fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, because I think people usually think of a benchmark as just a scoreboard. You build a dataset, you put up a leaderboard, and you see who's on top. And that's fine, that's one purpose, but honestly it's the one I find least interesting.

The thing I care most about is a benchmark as a way of defining the problem. When we were putting together something like SWE-bench, the real work wasn't collecting the GitHub issues. It was asking, what does it actually mean for a model to do software engineering? Does it have to run the tests? Does it have to navigate a repository with thousands of files? Does it have to figure out which files to even look at? Once you make those decisions concrete, you've basically written down a spec for a capability that didn't have a name before. And then the whole community can rally around it. People start building methods for it, people start arguing about it, and that argument is where the progress comes from.

The second thing, which is related, is that a good benchmark tells you where the model is actually breaking, not just whether it's good or bad. If you look at a task and the number is 40 percent, that's not very informative. But if you can slice it and say, okay, the failures are all in cases where the model needed to run something and look at the output and change its plan, now you've learned something about the model. That's the diagnostic purpose, and I think it's underrated.

And then I'll say one more thing, which is that I like benchmarks that are grounded in something real, where if a model does well, somebody's life actually gets a little easier. I've become less interested in tasks that are only hard in an academic sense. If the task resembles what a person does at work or in their daily life, then the benchmark score has some meaning outside of the research paper, and I think that's what keeps a benchmark relevant for more than a year or two.

r001.rationale: It contrasts benchmarks as leaderboards for ranking models with benchmarks that define a capability and help the community make progress on it.

r002.rationale: It discusses defining software-engineering tasks and diagnosing model failures, but does not clearly state a preference for benchmarks aimed at capabilities models currently lack or have not fully developed.

r003.rationale: It says a concrete benchmark can rally the community, prompting people to build methods and debate the capability, which drives progress.

opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few different purposes a benchmark can serve, and they get conflated a lot. One is purely diagnostic: you want to know whether your model can do X, so you build a test for X. That's useful, but it's not the one I find most exciting.

The purpose I find most interesting is a benchmark as a kind of north star. It's a way of saying to the whole community, "This is a problem that actually matters, and here's a concrete, measurable way to tell whether we're making progress on it." A good benchmark changes what people work on. If you look back at the history of the field, a lot of progress came from someone defining the right task at the right time, even more than from any single modeling idea. ImageNet is the classic example. It didn't just measure vision models. It reshaped what the field thought was possible and worth trying.

That's why, when we built things like SWE-bench, the goal wasn't to make a hard puzzle for its own sake. We wanted to take something people genuinely care about, like resolving real issues in real software repositories, and make it measurable. When we released it, models were solving a very small fraction of the problems. That was intentional. You want a benchmark with headroom, one that gives people a reason to build new systems, new agent scaffolds, new ways of using tools and interacting with environments, rather than squeezing out another half point on something that's already saturated.

The other piece I care a lot about now is reliability. As these models get deployed as agents that take actions on behalf of people, average accuracy isn't really the number you care about. You care whether the system does the right thing consistently, the tenth time and the hundredth time, when the user phrases things a bit differently or the situation is slightly unusual. A model that gets something right 60% of the time on a single try can look very different when you ask whether it gets it right every time across several tries. So I think one of the most important purposes of a benchmark today is to bring the evaluation closer to what deployment actually looks like: messy, interactive, multi-turn, with real consequences for getting it wrong.

So to sum it up, the purpose I find most interesting is a benchmark that's a step ahead of the field. It's grounded in something real, hard enough that it isn't solved yet, and designed so that making progress on it means you've built something more useful, not just something better at taking the test.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts diagnostic benchmarks with benchmarks that guide progress, but it does not identify ranking models as the first purpose.

r002.rationale: It favors benchmarks with headroom that models have not solved, giving the community a reason to develop new systems and capabilities.

r003.rationale: It says a good benchmark changes what the community works on and describes benchmarks as drawing effort toward meaningful, underdeveloped tasks.

fable-5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question to start with. I think the purpose I find most compelling is that a benchmark is really a way of defining a goal for the field — it's almost a statement about what we think matters. When you build a benchmark, you're not just measuring progress, you're actually steering it, because researchers will optimize for whatever you put in front of them.

So for me, the most interesting benchmarks are the ones that capture some capability we genuinely want from these systems in the real world, rather than just a proxy that's easy to measure. If you think about something like software engineering, for example — it's one thing to ask a model to complete a function in isolation, and it's a very different thing to ask it to go into a real codebase, understand the context, and resolve an actual issue. The second one is messier and harder to evaluate, but it's much closer to what we actually care about.

The other purpose I'd highlight is that a good benchmark tells you where the gaps are. When models saturate a benchmark quickly, you've learned something, but honestly the more valuable benchmarks are the ones where there's a lot of headroom — where the gap between current systems and humans, or current systems and what we'd want, is large and interpretable. That gap is what generates the next few years of research questions. So I tend to think of benchmarks less as leaderboards and more as instruments for discovering what we don't yet know how to do.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts benchmarks as leaderboards with benchmarks that steer researchers toward capabilities the field wants to develop.

r002.rationale: It prefers benchmarks with substantial headroom and interpretable gaps between current systems and desired capability.

r003.rationale: It says benchmarks steer researchers toward the measured goal and that capability gaps generate research questions.

opus-5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are really two very different things people mean by "benchmark," and I find one of them much more interesting than the other.

The first is measurement — you want a number that tells you whether model A is better than model B, you want to track progress over time, you want to decide what to ship. That's genuinely useful, I don't want to dismiss it, but it's kind of an engineering function. And it has this failure mode where the benchmark gets saturated, or contaminated, and then you're measuring something that's drifted away from what you actually cared about.

The thing I find much more interesting is a benchmark as an *articulation of a goal*. You're basically saying: here is a capability I believe matters, that I don't currently know how to build, and I'm going to write it down precisely enough that other people can attack it. That's a very different intellectual act. It's closer to writing a research agenda than to writing a test.

And the best ones have this property where failure is informative. If a model gets forty percent, you want to be able to look at the sixty percent and learn something structural about what's missing — not just "it's not smart enough yet." A lot of our work on interactive environments came from that frustration. With a static dataset, a model fails and you shrug. But when you put the model in an environment where it has to take actions, deal with a user who hasn't told it everything, recover from its own mistakes — the failures become legible. You can see it compounding errors, you can see it not asking the clarifying question.

So, measurement is the boring half. The interesting half is using a benchmark to make a vague intuition about intelligence into something concrete enough to be wrong about.

r001.rationale: It contrasts benchmarks used to compare models and track progress with benchmarks that articulate a goal for research.

r002.rationale: It favors benchmarks that specify a capability that matters but that the speaker does not yet know how to build.

r003.rationale: It says a benchmark can define a capability precisely enough for other people to work on it.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the most interesting purpose for a benchmark is to point the field at something we don't yet know how to do. A lot of benchmarks just measure progress on a problem we already understand, and those get saturated quickly. The ones I find exciting define a capability gap clearly enough that people can go after it, and the gap closes as a result.

For me that has meant benchmarks for language agents, where a model has to act in an environment over many steps instead of answering a single question. In that setting it isn't enough to be right once. The model has to plan, use tools, recover from mistakes, and stay consistent over a long interaction. When we built benchmarks like SWE-bench and τ-bench, we wanted them to look like real work: fixing an actual GitHub issue, or handling a customer request under a policy while a simulated user pushes back. Those tasks expose failures that a static question-answering benchmark would never show.

The second purpose I care about is reliability. It's easy to show that a model can sometimes do a task. It's much harder to show it can do the task every time, and that difference decides whether you'd actually trust it in deployment. So I like benchmarks that measure consistency across repeated attempts, not just a best-case score.

A good benchmark has to stay connected to what we actually want these systems to do. If it drifts into a puzzle that's only useful for leaderboard climbing, you end up optimizing for the wrong thing. So I'd say the best benchmark both tells you where we are and shapes where the research goes next.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts measuring progress on familiar tasks with shaping future research, but it does not clearly identify ranking models as the contrasting use.

r002.rationale: It prefers benchmarks that expose a capability gap in something models do not yet know how to do.

r003.rationale: It says benchmarks can point the field toward an unknown capability, prompting people to work on it until the gap closes.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the most useful benchmarks measure whether a system can actually get something done, not just whether it produces a plausible answer. Many early benchmarks rewarded pattern matching on a fixed test set, and once models got good at those, the scores told us less than we hoped. What interests me more is evaluation in interactive settings: give a model a goal, some tools, and an environment that pushes back, then see whether it plans well, recovers from mistakes, and knows when to ask for help. Those tasks say much more about reliability, which is what people care about when they deploy these systems.

I'd also want a benchmark to be hard to game. If the test leaks into training data or can be solved with a shortcut, the number stops meaning much. And when a model fails, the failure should be informative. A good benchmark tells you *why* something broke, not just that the score dropped.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts measuring real task performance with producing plausible answers and pattern matching, but it does not distinguish ranking models from using benchmarks to drive progress toward a capability.

r002.rationale: It prefers interactive benchmarks involving planning, recovery, and asking for help, but does not say these target capabilities models currently lack or have not fully developed.

r003.rationale: It does not describe introducing a benchmark to draw community effort toward an underexplored capability.

astra-6.text: I think the most interesting purpose of a benchmark is to help us figure out what to work on next. You can use it to rank systems, but a single score doesn’t necessarily tell you very much about why one system is better than another. What I find more useful is when a benchmark exposes a gap: a model does well in one setting, but you change something seemingly small and it struggles. Now you have a research question. What was it actually learning, and what capability is missing? A good benchmark gives you a way to investigate that and measure whether you’re making progress.

r001.rationale: It contrasts ranking systems with using benchmark-exposed gaps to identify research questions and measure progress.

r002.rationale: It favors benchmarks that reveal a model’s struggle and the capability it is missing.

r003.rationale: It says benchmarks can help identify what to work on next, but does not say introducing one draws community effort toward that capability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most interesting purpose of a benchmark is to help us figure out what we’re missing. You can use a benchmark to rank systems, which is useful, but I’m more interested in whether it reveals a capability we don’t yet know how to build.

Ideally, you look at where a model fails and learn something: is it struggling to reason, does it lack some knowledge, or can it just not apply what it knows in a new setting? Those suggest very different research directions. So, for me, a good benchmark doesn’t just tell you how well you’re doing. It helps you decide what question to work on next.

A good benchmark should push us beyond memorization, test reasoning and robustness, and help us understand where models fail so we can improve them. The score itself is less important than the insight it gives us.
